Profit does not equal cash in the bank.

A business can show an annual profit of $2.6M and still end up with $920K in actual cash. On paper, the earnings look strong. In reality, the cash is tied up elsewhere.

Receivables at $680K, inventory at $380K, capex at $310K, and debt repayment at $310K consume the difference. Small margin and price moves often change profit more than expected, but cash flow dictates how fast the business can actually move.

TaxBooksCFO helps owners track operating cash flow against net income to see where money goes. When that ratio sits under roughly 80% for two or more quarters, profit is stuck inside the operations.

Map the bridge from profit to cash for the last twelve months to find the biggest drain.

How much of your last year of profit is sitting in your bank account today?

Old receivables carry a hidden cost for growing companies.

When a balance sheet shows $1.45M in total receivables with $145K sitting past 90 days, cash flow slows down immediately. That 10% metric signals trouble before the bank balance does.

Owners often miss the warning signs hiding in the aging report. Watch for the same customers appearing on the overdue list month after month. Check if the reserve for doubtful accounts matches reality.

TaxBooksCFO helps owners review these numbers clearly and set firm collection standards. Stop new work and pause shipments to accounts over 90 days. Book an honest reserve for cash that will not arrive.

Stock is cash disguised as inventory.

Consider a business running at six million dollars a year. The daily cost of goods sits at sixteen thousand four hundred dollars. When inventory drifts upward by fifteen days, two hundred forty-seven thousand dollars of hard cash is removed from operations and converted into items sitting on a shelf.

Most owners spot inventory issues only after cash gets tight. The calculation is straightforward: divide inventory by cost of goods, then multiply by three hundred sixty-five. That ratio shows exactly how long capital remains trapped.

TaxBooksCFO advises owners to look for specific red flags. Check for items with no sale in six or more months. Watch if inventory grows faster than sales. Ensure reorder points reflect real sales data rather than guesswork.

Take action this week. Rank every SKU by days on hand. Discount or return the slow-moving tail. Reset reorder points based strictly on the last ninety days of activity.

Growth consumes cash long before it delivers profit.

Consider an $11M business growing 25%. That adds $2.75M in new revenue. If the operation requires 15% in working capital for every dollar of revenue, that expansion ties up $412K in cash. Receivables and inventory demand capital upfront before collections arrive.

TaxBooksCFO watches for working capital percentage rising alongside top-line expansion, as well as extending receivable or inventory days. Without adjustments, higher sales simply drain the bank account faster.

Size the capital requirement before signing new contracts. Multiply planned new revenue by the working capital percentage, then negotiate deposits, shorter terms, or milestone billing with customers.

Small timing shifts alter your entire cash position.

Consider a business with thirteen million dollars in annual revenue. That generates thirty-five thousand six hundred dollars in revenue per day. When customers take fifteen days longer to pay, five hundred thirty-four thousand dollars of cash leaves the bank account and sits in customer accounts instead.

Receivables, inventory, and payables dictate how fast a growing enterprise burns cash. Owners often watch profit and miss the working capital cycle entirely. Growth consumes cash before it shows up as earnings.

Look for days sales outstanding creeping fifteen days past standard terms. Watch for growing piles of invoices sitting past sixty days. Contrast that with accounts that stay tightly aligned with terms.

Fix the billing lag this week. Bill the moment work ships rather than waiting for month-end. Make the phone call at day thirty-one instead of sending another automated email. Require deposits or cards on file for new accounts.

Profit is not cash.

Cash goes negative in week 10. Would you know today? Most business owners look at monthly statements. Monthly statements hide timing. They tell you what happened, not what is coming.

TaxBooksCFO helps owners build a simple weekly view. Opening cash plus receipts minus payments, week by week. The math is straightforward. The perspective is different.

Look for three specific signals in the numbers. Watch for a negative week with nothing lined up to cover it. Watch for big payments clustered in the same week. Watch a minimum cash line you never cross.

Build the model once for thirteen weeks. Roll it weekly by dropping the past week and adding a new one. Act early by moving payments or drawing credit before the low week arrives.

Your P&L can look healthy while the business is getting weaker.

That usually happens when cash gets trapped somewhere between:

Revenue → Receivables → Inventory → Cash

A financial health review should answer five questions:

1. Is cash conversion improving?
2. Are margins holding?
3. Is working capital consuming more cash?
4. Can debt service be covered without stress?
5. Can management forecast the next 90–180 days?

If the answer to any of those is unclear, the issue is not the spreadsheet.

It is visibility.

We are opening financial health reviews for business owners who want a clear view before the problem becomes expensive.

When books close 19 days after month-end, the information arrives too late to guide current decisions. An owner cannot steer operations using reports from three weeks ago.

A small dip in margin quietly drains cash.

Consider an annual revenue of $12M. A gross margin loss of 3% seems minor on a dashboard, but it represents $360K of profit gone every year.

Gross margin is calculated as (Revenue − cost of goods) ÷ revenue. Margin drift usually happens in silence. It occurs when supplier increases are absorbed without repricing, or when margin varies a lot month to month without being questioned.

TaxBooksCFO recommends tracking gross margin by product line every month. Flag any line down a point from its average, and build supplier cost increases into prices quickly.

A 7% budget miss rarely announces itself loudly.

Consider a monthly budgeted profit of $360K against an actual profit of $335K. On paper, it looks like a small gap. But when nobody notices for 60 days, that variance quietly compounds into a serious blind spot.

Calculate the variance line by line using (Actual − budget) ÷ budget. Watch closely if the same line misses 3 months in a row, and never settle for variances explained only at year-end. Each big variance needs an owner and an concrete action.

TaxBooksCFO advises owners to build a simple habit this week. Pick 5 lines: Revenue, gross margin, payroll and the two biggest costs. Review them within 10 days of month-end, and reforecast the rest of the year when reality changes.

Lenders do not look at net income first.

They look at the debt service coverage ratio. In this example, the business generates $864K in cash available for debt service against $600K in annual principal and interest, resulting in a 1.44x DSCR.

Lenders look for comfortable headroom above your covenant. Coverage falling two quarters in a row signals operational friction long before a cash shortfall occurs. Falling near or below your covenant level immediately changes how a lender treats your business.

TaxBooksCFO advises owners to find the loan agreement and confirm how the covenant is measured. Compute it monthly on a rolling 12-month basis. If coverage drops, call early, because lenders prefer a heads-up to a surprise.

Break-even is the most important line on your financial statement.

Take an illustrative company with $2.3M in annual fixed costs and a 45% contribution margin. That business needs $5.11M in revenue just to stand still.

Most owners focus entirely on top-line revenue. Revenue is vanity. A small shift in your margin changes your profit far more than an increase in gross sales. When you know your exact break-even point, you stop guessing.

Watch for three specific signals. Check if your break-even is rising faster than your revenue. Look for fixed costs added for growth that has not arrived yet. Measure the exact gap between current sales and break-even.

TaxBooksCFO helps owners build clarity around these numbers so decisions are grounded in reality rather than hope. Split your costs into fixed and variable line by line this week. Compute your break-even using the simple formula of fixed costs divided by contribution margin. Recheck it every quarter because every new hire and lease moves the line.
